newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Striking Russia energy workers get back-pay pledge.
newsitem.headline: Striking Russia energy workers get back-pay pledge.

text.p: The governor of Russia's Far East region, where thousands of power workers are on strike over unpaid wages, said on Tuesday a local financial crisis could be resolved by the middle of next month.
Strikers blacked out parts of the region on Monday, halving electricity output to protest that they had not been paid for months.
Yevgeny Nazdratenko, under pressure from President Boris Yeltsin to end the industrial unrest, told a news conference in Moscow that he was about to sign a deal to unravel a knot of mutual debts.

"I think within two or three weeks this problem will be solved," he told a news conference after flying in from Primorsky Krai, a region of more than two million people which includes the major Pacific port of Vadivostok.
But he gave no details of how to solve the crisis, which critics say is too complicated to settle immediately.

Union leaders said more than 10,000 of the region's 17,000 energy workers had joined the strike, which began this week and has left whole residential areas and dozens of industrial enterprises without power.
The number of strikers could not be independently confirmed but the impact of the strike on the local economy and population has been limited because power cuts were already frequent.
Nazdratenko has blamed Moscow for the payments crisis, in which some workers have not been paid since April. He said he expected an agreement on clearing the debts to be signed later on Tuesday.
But asked specifically when workers would get paid, the governor was vague. "When mutual debts are cleared in our country," he said.
A spokesman for the Energy Ministry said he did not know of any comprehensive deal being signed. "Different consultations are being held but the matter is very complicated," he said.
On Monday strikers scorned Nazdratenko's offer to resolve the crisis within two weeks if the strike was put on hold.
Their leaders in Vladivostok -- seven time zones east of Moscow -- were not immediately available for comment on the governor's latest statements.

Under pressure over the industrial unrest, Nazdratenko had called for a region-wide referendum on his actions on September 22, but on Tuesday he said it should be called off because the problems were being solved.
Strike leader Gennady Tkachuk said workers at utility Dalenergo, which supplies Vladivostok, were owed 130 billion roubles ($24 million).
Workers at Primorsky hydroelectric station, where he said more than 100 people were on a hunger strike, were owed more than 30 billion roubles ($6 million).
Nazdratenko said unpaid debts by the defence plants in the heavily-militarised region -- closed to foreigners under communism -- were to blame for the crisis.

Former acting prime minister Yegor Gaidar, who pioneered Russia's market reforms, said in a radio interview that he believed the governor was to blame for keeping electricity prices artificially low in order to gain popularity.
